title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Splinting and Injection in Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with suspected mild or moderate carpal tunnel syndrome in primary care: clinical diagnosis, risk factors including diabetes and thyroid disease, who needs nerve conduction studies, night splinting, a single corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel with injection technique and safety, work adaptation, and when to refer for surgical decompression. Uses a primary care randomised trial (INSTINCTS) and a primary care clinical review; a Saudi cross-sectional study supplies local prevalence; no Saudi national guideline for carpal tunnel syndrome was found.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi professional society guideline for carpal tunnel syndrome was found; the INSTINCTS trial (England) and a 2015 primary care review (France) are the clinical sources and the Tabuk survey (2024) supplies Saudi prevalence only.
NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries could not be read from outside the United Kingdom; the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guideline was not retrieved.

The review gives two thresholds for referral for nerve conduction studies and surgery in persistent symptoms: 3 months of conservative treatment in one section and 1 month in another; the 6-week reassessment used in the trial is written as the first review and the conflict is flagged for clinician decision.

The 20 mg methylprednisolone acetate dose is from the INSTINCTS trial (given as 0.5 mL of a 40 mg/mL suspension); the Depo-Medrol label gives 4 to 30 mg for tendon sheath conditions and no carpal tunnel specific dose.

Triamcinolone acetonide is named in the review as an alternative with a longer half-life, but no carpal tunnel dose was found and the Kenalog-10 label gives intra-articular doses only; no triamcinolone regimen is written.

The review describes injecting the steroid with 1 mL of 1% lidocaine; the INSTINCTS trial gave no local anaesthetic; compatibility of mixing lidocaine and methylprednisolone in one syringe was not stated by the Depo-Medrol label and is not written as an instruction.
Oral corticosteroids, anti-inflammatory tablets, ultrasound-guided injection, hydrodissection and surgical technique are described only as options; no regimen is written.
Analgesics (paracetamol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) were allowed in the trial; no analgesic regimen is written.
Nerve conduction study thresholds and normal values vary by laboratory; no numeric cut-off is written.
Differentials and patient advice follow standard practice and were not drawn from a single source section.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web pages and label text; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: The median nerve runs through the carpal tunnel, a space bounded by the carpal bones at the back and the flexor retinaculum in front; anything that raises pressure or reduces space can squeeze the nerve (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Introduction). Pressure is highest with the wrist bent, so symptoms are worse at night and with sustained postures such as driving, and are partly relieved by shaking the hand or changing wrist position (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care). A night splint holds the wrist near neutral, which reduces pressure in the tunnel while the patient sleeps (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures). A corticosteroid injected next to the nerve reduces swelling in the tunnel and gives faster relief than a splint at 6 weeks, but the difference is small by 6 months (INSTINCTS trial, Section Findings and Section Discussion). Diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, obesity, renal failure and wrist fracture raise the risk; in a Saudi survey chronic disease raised the odds of carpal tunnel syndrome more than six-fold (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What are the Known Risk Factors?; Tabuk study, Section Abstract). Prolonged compression can cause permanent nerve damage with thenar muscle wasting, which is why severe symptoms need early specialist referral (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).

symptoms: Numbness, tingling or aching pain in the hand, especially at night, with clumsiness or weakness of grip (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care).
Symptoms worse with driving, holding a phone or repeated hand use, eased by shaking the hand (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care).

Symptoms from the palm to the fingertips, including the middle finger, often in both hands and sometimes radiating to the elbow (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care).
Isolated pain on the ulnar or back of the hand makes carpal tunnel syndrome unlikely (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care).
physicalSigns: Thenar muscle wasting or weakness of thumb abduction (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).
Reduced sensation in the thumb, index, middle finger and radial half of the ring finger (Tabuk study, Section Introduction).
Phalen and Tinel tests are neither sensitive nor specific; Phalen sensitivity 10 to 73% and specificity 55 to 86% (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).
Elbow, Guyon canal, tendon and neck tests to exclude other causes (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).
redFlags: Thenar wasting, weakness, or constant sensory loss: severe carpal tunnel syndrome needing nerve conduction studies and hand specialist referral (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).

Uncertain diagnosis, or symptoms beyond the median nerve area: nerve conduction studies and specialist referral (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What to do in Case of an Uncertain Diagnosis or Severe CTS?).
Pain or tingling spreading with neck movements or arm elevation: consider cervical spine disease or thoracic outlet syndrome (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).
Hot, red, swollen wrist or fever: consider infection or inflammatory arthritis and do not inject (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings: Immunosuppression and Increased Risk of Infection).

Symptoms persisting after a trial of conservative treatment: refer for nerve conduction studies and discuss surgical decompression (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Surgical decompression (patient information)).
precipitants: Pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, renal failure, wrist fracture and aromatase inhibitor treatment (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What are the Known Risk Factors?).
Manual work such as manufacturing, construction, food processing and vibrating tools (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What are the Known Risk Factors?).
Chronic disease: adjusted odds ratio 6.37 in Tabuk (Tabuk study, Section Abstract).
Female sex and older age (Tabuk study, Section Introduction).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Neck pain and symptoms reproduced by neck movement, spread beyond the median nerve area (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Little finger and ring finger numbness; positive elbow flexion test or Guyon canal tapping (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

Symptoms with arm elevation (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Both feet or hands involved in a glove-and-stocking pattern, with abnormal glucose or thyroid tests (Tabuk study, Section Abstract).

clinicalManagement.title: Make the clinical diagnosis
actions: Ask about night numbness, tingling, clumsiness, shaking the hand and activities such as driving (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Usual Clinical Presentation in Primary Care).
Examine the thenar muscles and sensation and test elbow, Guyon canal and neck to exclude other causes (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).
Check glucose, thyroid and kidney function; ask about pregnancy and rheumatoid arthritis (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What are the Known Risk Factors?).

If mild and typical with no differential diagnosis, start treatment without further tests (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer severe or uncertain cases
actions: Arrange nerve conduction studies and refer to a hand specialist for thenar weakness, sensory loss, major functional limitation, poor prognostic factors or an uncertain diagnosis (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What to do in Case of an Uncertain Diagnosis or Severe CTS?).

clinicalManagement.title: Offer splint or injection by patient preference
actions: Explain both options: the choice depends mainly on patient preference (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Conclusion).
A single injection gives faster relief at 6 weeks; by 6 months the results are similar (INSTINCTS trial, Section Findings and Section Discussion).
Prefer injection in pregnancy because symptoms usually resolve after delivery; take care in diabetes because glucose rises (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).

clinicalManagement.title: Fit a night splint
actions: Use a removable wrist brace that holds the wrist in neutral, adjusted to neutral before fitting because shop splints are often sold extended (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Nocturnal splinting).
Wear it every night for 6 weeks and do gentle wrist movements when it is removed (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).
Splints help most when the patient is woken at night by paraesthesia; daytime wear is not advised (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Nocturnal splinting).

clinicalManagement.title: Give a corticosteroid injection
actions: Use a sterile no-touch technique; insert a 23G to 25G needle at the wrist between the proximal and distal wrist creases, at 30 to 45 degrees, between palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris, and do not inject into the palm (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures; Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
Stop and reposition for severe pain, paraesthesia, blood on aspiration or resistance (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
Inject 20 mg methylprednisolone acetate (see medicines) (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).
Ask the patient to wait 30 minutes and rest the arm for 48 hours (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).

clinicalManagement.title: Adapt work and activities
actions: Discuss temporary changes of tasks, more rest breaks and tool changes for workers with vibrating tools or firm grip (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Work adaptation).
A short sick leave of under 2 weeks may be needed for heavy manual workers (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Work adaptation).

clinicalManagement.title: Review and escalate
actions: Review at 6 weeks, the time when further treatment is considered in primary care (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).
If symptoms persist or recur, refer for nerve conduction studies and discuss surgical decompression (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Surgical decompression (patient information)).
After surgery advise avoiding a firm grip for 6 weeks (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Surgical decompression (patient information)).

regimens.indication: Short-term relief of mild or moderate carpal tunnel syndrome
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with mild or moderate carpal tunnel syndrome
regimens.dose: 20 mg as a single injection (0.5 mL of the 40 mg/mL suspension) (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures); the label range for tendon sheath conditions is 4 to 30 mg (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration). Dilution and preparation: none; use the suspension as supplied; clean the vial top with povidone-iodine before aspiration and use strict aseptic technique (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
regimens.route: Local injection into the carpal tunnel through a 23G or 25G needle at the wrist between the proximal and distal wrist creases; not intravenous, not intrathecal, not epidural; no palm injection (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures; Depo-Medrol label, Boxed statement and Contraindications)
regimens.duration: One injection; effect lasts weeks, recurrence is common, repeat only after review (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection)
adjustments: Diabetes: glucose rises and antidiabetic doses may need adjustment; injection is not a good first choice (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection; Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions: Antidiabetics).
Pregnancy: injection is particularly effective because symptoms usually resolve after delivery (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
Live vaccines are contraindicated at immunosuppressive doses; hepatitis B carriers may reactivate with immunosuppressive dosages (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
CYP3A4 inducers can reduce the effect of corticosteroids (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Pain, bleeding or paraesthesia during injection: stop and reposition (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
Median nerve injury is uncommon (under 0.01%) but can cause lasting sensory loss; refer if suspected (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
Wait 30 minutes after injection; rest the arm for 48 hours (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).
Blood glucose in diabetes for several days (Depo-Medrol label, Drug Interactions).
Signs of infection or post-injection flare at the site (Depo-Medrol label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to methylprednisolone or any component (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura for intramuscular preparations (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Premature infants because of benzyl alcohol (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).
Acute local infection at the injection site (Depo-Medrol label, Warnings).
Systemic fungal infection, except intra-articular injection for a local joint condition (Depo-Medrol label, Contraindications).

regimens.dose: 1 mL of 1% lidocaine (10 mg) at the injection site (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection); the trial gave no local anaesthetic (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures). Dilution and preparation: none; use the 1% solution as supplied; do not exceed the label maximum dose.
regimens.route: Local infiltration at the injection site; aspirate before injecting to avoid intravascular injection (Xylocaine label, Warnings and Precautions)
regimens.frequency: Single dose with the steroid injection
adjustments: Use caution in severe liver disease (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Methaemoglobinaemia risk with other oxidising drugs (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Compatibility of mixing with methylprednisolone in one syringe was not stated by the Depo-Medrol label; give separately unless local protocol allows (Depo-Medrol label, Dosage and Administration).

monitoring: Signs of toxicity: perioral numbness, dizziness, tinnitus, convulsions (Xylocaine label, Adverse Reactions).
Temporary numbness can mask pain from a mis-sited needle; check for severe pain or paraesthesia before injecting (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Steroid injection).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anaesthetics (Xylocaine label, Contraindications).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Clinical diagnosis of mild and suggestive carpal tunnel syndrome
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Typical symptoms, no severe symptom and no other diagnosis after examination: no further investigation needed (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).
Thenar weakness, sensory deficit, or major limitation of daily activities or work (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).
Adult with a new episode of idiopathic mild or moderate carpal tunnel syndrome of at least 6 weeks (INSTINCTS trial, Section Methods).
Worn at night for 6 weeks with the wrist in neutral or slightly extended (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).
One injection of 20 mg methylprednisolone acetate into the carpal tunnel (INSTINCTS trial, Section Procedures).

Uncertain diagnosis, severe symptoms, or persistent symptoms after conservative treatment: nerve conduction studies and hand specialist (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What to do in Case of an Uncertain Diagnosis or Severe CTS?).

teaching.scope: Adult with suspected mild or moderate carpal tunnel syndrome in primary care: clinical diagnosis, risk factors including diabetes and thyroid disease, who needs nerve conduction studies, night splinting, a single corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel with injection technique and safety, work adaptation, and when to refer for surgical decompression. Uses a primary care randomised trial (INSTINCTS) and a primary care clinical review; a Saudi cross-sectional study supplies local prevalence; no Saudi national guideline for carpal tunnel syndrome was found.
learningObjectives: Diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome clinically and check diabetes, thyroid and kidney function.
Refer severe or uncertain cases for nerve conduction studies.
Offer a night splint or a single steroid injection by patient preference.
Review at 6 weeks and refer for surgery if symptoms persist.
keyPoints: Typical mild cases need no further tests.
Splint at night in neutral for 6 weeks; injection gives faster relief at 6 weeks.
Inject at the wrist crease, never into the palm, and stop for severe pain or paraesthesia.

patientEducation: Wear the splint every night for 6 weeks and take it off for gentle wrist movements.
After an injection rest the arm for 48 hours and wait 30 minutes before leaving.
Tell us if you have fever, redness or swelling at the wrist, or new numbness that does not improve.
If you have diabetes check your blood sugar more often for a few days after an injection.
Come back at 6 weeks; if symptoms remain you may need nerve tests or surgery.
lifestyleAndDiet: Take regular breaks from repeated hand tasks and vibrating tools.
Keep the wrist straight while driving and holding a phone.
Control diabetes and thyroid disease and keep a healthy weight.
Shake or move the hand when symptoms start.
Discuss task changes with your employer.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; musculoskeletal physician or physiotherapist; occupational health; hand surgeon; neurophysiologist; endocrinologist; pharmacist.
dischargeCriteria: Diagnosis, severity and risk factor tests documented; treatment chosen and explained; splint fitted or injection given with technique and consent recorded; advice on work and diabetes given; review at 6 weeks booked; criteria for earlier return and referral explained.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 6 weeks for symptoms and function; nerve conduction studies and hand surgery referral for severe, uncertain or persistent symptoms; repeat injection only after review; check glucose and thyroid results.
